# Audit Workflow

Goal: keep KeystoneOS useful instead of letting it become stale.

Two different questions, two different cadences. Confusing them is how a system stays "well maintained" and still gives wrong answers.

| Question | Tool | Cadence |
|---|---|---|
| Is it **built right**? (structure, coverage) | Four Cs audit, below | Weekly |
| Is it **still true**? (drift, freshness) | `.\scripts\keystone.ps1 freshness` | Every morning, automatic |
| Am I **still doing the rituals**? | `.\scripts\ritual-check.ps1` | Every morning + `KeystoneOS-Rituals` nudge |
| Is it *deeply* still true? (6-check deep audit) | `os-audit` skill | Quarterly |

**Why the ritual check exists.** A skipped ritual produces no error — it produces an absence, and absences are invisible. `interview-me` and `weekly-review` both stopped on 2026-06-05 and nothing noticed for 49 days while every cron-driven surface stayed green. The check reads each ritual's own output as the record of when it last ran (a state file can drift from reality; the artifact cannot).

## Daily — automatic

`freshness` runs inside the morning cadence. It checks hand-written surface age (30-day budget), routing integrity, unmapped top-level folders, root hygiene, stale worktrees, and audit cadence. Output lands in `outputs/morning/cadence.log`. It never fails the cadence — read it, don't rely on it shouting.

Run it manually any time: `.\scripts\keystone.ps1 freshness`, or `freshness -Sweep` to also remove worktrees whose content already landed on main. Locked worktrees are always respected.

## Weekly — Four Cs Audit

Score each out of 25:

- **Context:** current user, priorities, project briefs, decisions. Is `context/priorities.md` still true this week?
- **Connections:** reachable systems. Verify with the check commands in `connections.md` rather than trusting what's written there.
- **Capabilities:** workflows, scripts, skills, harness adapters. Do the three harness adapters still agree?

| Job | Normal time | Run it now |
|---|---|---|

**See if a job is loaded and what it returned last time:**

Column 2 is the last exit code. `0` is good. Anything else means that job died quietly.

# Forecast Capture

Freezes cfbvictorymodel.com's forecasts for the coming weekend, then reports
what changed. Takes no arguments and asks nothing — Baylor and 2026 are the
defaults and rarely change.

## Why this exists

The report's "Chance of Victory" column is **overwritten with the realised
result** once a game is played. Across 2019–2025 that destroyed every pre-game
probability the model ever produced. Miss a week and that week's forecast is
gone permanently — it cannot be recovered later. This makes 2026 the first
gradable season.

## Run it

```powershell
cd /Users/kristinarash/DEV/CFB_Victory_Model
python3 weekly_capture.py --team Baylor --year 2026
python3 compare_snapshots.py --team Baylor
```

Then read the comparison output back to the user in plain language (see below).

**Must run headed.** A Chrome window will open — that is expected, not a bug.
In headless mode Power BI's virtualised slicer list never renders past the
first ~8 alphabetical teams and Baylor is unreachable. Do not add `--headless`.

`Team attempt 1 failed, retrying...` in the output is **normal** — the first
slicer interaction races the app's own start-up. It retries 3×. Only treat it
as a failure if all attempts are exhausted.

## What to report back

Lead with whether the capture succeeded and the game count, then:

=== hook timeout cap ===
---
name: memsearch-hook-timeout-cap
description: "the SessionEnd memsearch hook's fixed 45s cap was outrun by corpus growth, so every session-end index timed out and incremental recall silently degraded to the 09:00 nightly; fixed 2026-09-02 by detaching the indexer"
metadata: 
  node_type: memory
  type: project
  modified: 2026-09-02T12:33:29.526Z
  originSessionId: 00fe7fc2-f53c-471d-b407-c777e8cc679c
---

`~/.claude/hooks/memsearch-sync.js` (SessionEnd) ran `memsearch index <10 paths>` through
`spawnSync` with a **45s cap**, sized in July against a "~17s fixed floor, ~5s incremental"
measurement. Measured again 2026-09-02 against the current corpus (~1,450 files;
`SecondBrain/Inbox/meetings` alone is 593 and `SecondBrain/Knowledge` 334):

| run | time |
|---|---|
| no-op, nothing new to embed | **33s** (was ~17s) |
| one day of accumulated content | **278s** (232 chunks, ~1s/chunk) |

So the cap left ~12s of embedding budget — under a dozen new chunks. **Every ordinary
session-end index was timing out.** Incremental indexing had quietly degraded to "whatever
the 09:00 nightly full reindex picks up", leaving search up to 24h stale.

**Why it stayed invisible for weeks.** Three dampers stacked:
`daily-backup.ps1` resets `.memsearch-timeout-streak` every morning, the escalation
threshold is 6 consecutive timeouts, and the hook writes only to `.memsearch-index.log`
below that. So a normal day of 2-4 session-ends never reached the threshold and never
surfaced. It took **six session-ends inside 47 minutes** (2026-09-01, 21:09-21:56) to
produce a 7-long streak and one `.errors.log` line. The alarm fired on burst *frequency*,
never on the underlying constant failure.

**The misread that line invites:** ETIMEDOUT + a clustered burst pattern-matches
[[milvus-lock-misdiagnosis]] (session-end lock contention), and the hook's own comments
say exactly that. It was not contention — `pgrep`/`lsof` showed no holder and the DB was
healthy. **Time the actual command before believing the comment.**

**Fix (2026-09-02): detached background worker.** The hook now re-execs itself as
`node memsearch-sync.js --worker` with `detached: true, stdio: 'ignore'` and `.unref()`,
then exits — measured **42ms**. The worker keeps the entire original body, so it owns the
PID lock (clustered session-ends still elect one indexer), writes `INDEX_LOG`, and runs
every error branch. Its `spawnSync` cap is now 600s: a runaway guard, not a budget, so an
ETIMEDOUT there genuinely means ">10 minutes".

- `stdio: 'ignore'` is **not optional** — inherited or piped stdio keeps the harness's pipe
  open and it waits for the child anyway, rebuilding the timeout with extra steps.
- Self-respawn, **not** an `sh -c` wrapper: the wrapper would discard the lock ownership
  and all four error-classification branches.
- The old header justified staying synchronous with a **Windows** process-group race.
  That rationale died with the 2026-08-05 migration; the comment now says so, because the
  next reader would otherwise "restore" the bug.

**How to apply:**
- A fixed timeout sized against a measured corpus is a **dated** number. When the corpus is
  something that grows every day (the vault, meetings, dailies), the cap has an expiry date
  nobody writes down. Prefer detaching over raising a cap; if a cap must stay, record the
  measurement and the date beside it so drift is visible.
- Never size a SessionEnd hook to block. Session teardown cannot wait minutes, so any
  design where "correct" means minutes must be asynchronous.
- Both harnesses wire their own copy. `~/.codex/hooks/memsearch-sync.js` is now a
  **symlink** to the Claude copy (2026-09-02) so the pair cannot drift again — same fix as
  `~/.codex/AGENTS.md`. Before "fixing a hook", ask which copy the harness wires; see
  [[memsearch-index-path-drift]] for the four-copy history.
- `~/DEV/KeystoneOS/scripts/codex-hooks/memsearch-sync.ps1` still has a 45s
  `WaitForExit(45000)`, but nothing wires it (Codex uses `hooks.json` → the `.js`). Dead
  Windows-era code; left alone deliberately.

name: memsearch-index-path-drift
description: "the SessionEnd memsearch hook read its path config from a Windows-era ~/Desktop/DEV path and silently fell back, indexing 4 of 10 memory paths for months after the Mac migration"
metadata: 
  node_type: memory
  type: project
  modified: 2026-08-15T04:07:30.329Z
  originSessionId: 75381393-88b6-4b65-960d-6613e08f7060
---

Three writers read it: the SessionEnd hook `~/.claude/hooks/memsearch-sync.js`, `~/.claude/scripts/daily-backup.ps1` (nightly; 09:00 since 2026-08-29), and the Codex hook `KeystoneOS/scripts/codex-hooks/memsearch-sync.ps1`.

**Found 2026-08-14:** the JS hook pointed at `~/Desktop/DEV/KeystoneOS/data/memory-index-paths.json` — the pre-migration Windows layout. DEV lives at `~/DEV` on this Mac, so the read threw, the `catch` returned a hardcoded fallback, and the hook indexed **4 paths instead of 10** for months. So only the JS hook drifted — and it is the one wired into `settings.json` (`SessionEnd`, 50s timeout).

Unindexed as a result: `SecondBrain/Knowledge`, `SecondBrain/Inbox/meetings`, `SecondBrain/morning-briefings`, the Mac memory slug `-Users-kristinarash-DEV/memory`, `KeystoneOS/decisions`, `.codex/memories`. Incremental recall for all of those depended entirely on that nightly.

A silent `catch → fallback` means a migration-broken config path degrades into a quieter, smaller, still-succeeding job — no error, no log line, no failed run. Nothing surfaces until someone asks "why didn't that turn up in search?" The bug was not the wrong path; it was that the wrong path cost nothing to have.

- Any config-file fallback in this stack must log to `.errors.log` when it fires. The JS hook now does. A fallback that never announces itself is a silent outage with a long tail.
- When auditing post-migration breakage, grep for `Desktop/DEV` and `Desktop/SecondBrain` — those two strings mark Windows-era assumptions. Do not trust that a script "works" as evidence its paths resolved; check what it actually resolved to.
- Verify path config by resolving it in isolation (`node -e` reading the same JSON, printing EXISTS/MISSING per entry) rather than by running the indexer — that proves the fix without taking the Milvus Lite write lock.

Adding a `logErr()` call inside `resolvePaths` therefore hit the const temporal dead zone, and `logErr`'s own `try/catch` swallowed the ReferenceError — reproducing the silent fallback the fix was meant to remove. `ERR_LOG` must be declared before `PATHS`.

**A THIRD hook had the same stale path, found 2026-09-01 during `/doctor-plus`.** `~/.claude/hooks/keystone-unified-snapshot.js` (SessionStart) read `~/Desktop/DEV/KeystoneOS/outputs/dashboard/unified-snapshot.md`, threw ENOENT, and its `catch (_) { emit(null) }` injected **nothing at all** — for every session since the migration. The snapshot file was being written correctly the whole time at `~/DEV/KeystoneOS/outputs/dashboard/`; only the reader was wrong. Zero symptoms: no error, no log, valid JSON on stdout, session starts normally.

The 2026-08-14/15 sweep fixed the two `memsearch-sync.js` copies but did not catch this one, so **"grep for `Desktop/DEV`" must cover every file in `~/.claude/hooks/` and `~/.codex/hooks/`, not only the hook currently being repaired.** Run it as a sweep across the whole hooks tree, not per-file.

That sweep then found a **fourth** copy — `~/.codex/hooks/keystone-unified-snapshot.js`, byte-identical and wired in `~/.codex/hooks.json`. Also fixed 2026-09-01.

**A second signature the `Desktop/DEV` grep cannot catch:** `~/.codex/AGENTS.md` (dated 2026-08-08) had been through a bad `claude` to `Codex` find-replace, so it told Codex to read `~/.Codex/global-memory/`, `~/.Codex/projects/<slug>/memory/` and `~/.Codex/Codex-memory-compiler/daily/` — none of which exist. Grep for `.Codex` (capital C) as well as `Desktop/DEV` when auditing migration damage. Also check which AGENTS.md the harness actually reads: `~/.claude/AGENTS.md` was correct but referenced by nothing.

Resolved 2026-09-01: `~/.codex/AGENTS.md` is now a symlink to `~/.claude/AGENTS.md`, so the pair has one home and cannot drift again. `setup-agents-symlinks.sh` was also sourcing `CLAUDE.md` for that link — the one thing `CLAUDE.md` explicitly forbids — and now sources `AGENTS.md`. Running that script used to recreate the bug.

Repaired 2026-09-01: path corrected to `~/DEV`, required sources now push a visible "SessionStart hook could not read a required memory file" block into `additionalContext` instead of failing silently, and the hook now also injects `global-memory/USER.md` + `MEMORY.md` (replacing a prose rule in `CLAUDE.md` that nothing enforced). The KeystoneOS snapshot is pointed at, not pasted.

Related: [[milvus-lock-misdiagnosis]] (found while fixing that), [[project_secondbrain-vault-location]] (the vault move that stranded the fallback), [[backup-sync-system]]

---
name: project_memory-compiler-pipeline
description: How the claude-memory-compiler flush/index pipeline fails and how to tell which stage broke; SessionStart injection was rewritten to a pointer 2026-08-29
metadata: 
  node_type: memory
  type: project
  originSessionId: 174cde34-d23d-454b-8db8-9365e7f728f2
  modified: 2026-08-29T20:05:21.521Z
---

The compiler at `~/.claude/claude-memory-compiler/` has three stages. Each fails
differently and the symptoms look alike, so identify the stage before fixing.

**Stage 1 — `hooks/session-end.py`.** Writes `scripts/session-flush-<uuid>-<YYYYMMDD>-<HHMMSS>.md`,
then spawns `flush.py`. Logs every firing to `scripts/flush.log` as `SessionEnd fired`.
If `flush.log` has no such line for days but the hook works when run by hand, sessions
are being *closed* rather than exited cleanly — not a config break. Self-verifying: end
one session normally and re-check the tail.

**Stage 2 — `scripts/flush.py`.** Calls the Agent SDK, appends to `daily/<date>.md`, writes
`scripts/last-flush.json` **only on success**, and **deletes its context file on success**.
Therefore **every leftover `session-flush-*.md` is a flush that died**, and its datestamp
maps to a missing `daily/<date>.md`. That is the cheapest diagnostic in the whole system —
count the leftovers. A stale `last-flush.json` means flushes are *dying*, not that the hook
never fired. Recover one by hand:
`uv run --directory ~/.claude/claude-memory-compiler python scripts/flush.py <context-file> <session-id> [YYYY-MM-DD]`
Success = `Result: FLUSH_OK` + `Flush complete` in `flush.log`.

**The third arg is a backfill date, added 2026-08-29.** Without it `flush.py` always writes
to *today's* log, so recovering old stranded files silently misfiles them under the current
date. Always pass the date parsed from the filename when backfilling; entries are then
marked `(backfilled …)`.

**Batch-recovery trap — the 60-second dedup guard destroys data.** `flush.py` skips a run
whose `session_id` matches `last-flush.json` within 60s, and **deletes the context file on
that skip path too**. One session can have several stranded files (different timestamps), so
a loop that hits the same uuid twice inside a minute silently loses the second one — it still
prints as consumed. Hit 2026-08-29: 12 files ran, 10 flushed, 2 dropped. Before trusting a

**Public skills (`TitleCase`) ship to the world. Private skills (`_ALLCAPS`) never leave the local repo.** Sensitivity is decided by skill name, not by per-file scrubbing at share-time.

### The Bright Line

**Public skill (`TitleCase`) — content rule:**

ONLY templated, safe, public, ready content. Period.

- ✅ Generic instructions any LifeOS user could follow
- ✅ Templated patterns with placeholders for user-specific values
- ✅ Public API references and dependencies on public tools
- ❌ Real names (people, products, companies, customers)
- ❌ Real domains, hostnames, IPs, internal URLs
- ❌ API keys, tokens, credentials, session cookies, OAuth secrets — even example-looking ones
- ❌ Private repo paths or references (`github.com/<org>/<private-repo>`)
- ❌ Customer data, customer-specific workflows, customer engagement context
- ❌ First-person war stories tied to a specific incident, project, or person
- ❌ User-specific filesystem paths (`/Users/<name>/...`, `/home/<name>/...`)
- ❌ Identity-bound preferences (DA name, principal name, partner name, pet name, financial figures, health data)

**Private skill (`_ALLCAPS`) — content rule:**

Anything goes. Real names, real domains, real customers, real credentials-by-reference (env var names, never values), real war stories, real internal infra. The underscore IS the safety boundary. These skills are excluded from release tooling.

### The Decision Test

When you find yourself wanting to write any of the following into a skill body, that skill MUST be `_ALLCAPS`:

| If the skill mentions… | Skill must be |
|------------------------|---------------|
| A specific person's name (yours, your partner's, your team's, a customer's) | `_ALLCAPS` |
| A specific product name you own or sell | `_ALLCAPS` |
| A specific customer or client | `_ALLCAPS` |
| A specific paid API account, billing realm, or subscription | `_ALLCAPS` |
| A specific private domain, hostname, internal IP, or VPN | `_ALLCAPS` |
| A specific private repo, dotfile location, or local infra | `_ALLCAPS` |
| A specific business process tied to your company | `_ALLCAPS` |
| A specific financial, health, security, or legal context | `_ALLCAPS` |
| A specific incident or one-off war story | `_ALLCAPS` |
| Anything that would be wrong, embarrassing, or unsafe in someone else's `~/.claude/` | `_ALLCAPS` |

If none of the above apply and the skill is fully generic — it can be `TitleCase` (public).

### Where Personal Layering Goes for Public Skills

A public skill can be made user-specific at runtime via `~/.claude/LIFEOS/USER/CUSTOMIZATIONS/SKILLS/<SkillName>/PREFERENCES.md`. The skill body stays generic; the user's customization file overlays per-instance context. Use this when a skill is fundamentally generic but benefits from per-user tweaks (preferred voice, default formats, personal taste).

**Do not use SKILLCUSTOMIZATIONS to smuggle private content into a public skill.** If the skill *requires* private context to function (real customer name, real API account, real internal infra), it is a private skill — name it `_ALLCAPS` and stop.

### Allowed in Public Skills

- Generic `~/` paths (`~/.claude/skills/`, `~/Projects/<tool>/`) — resolve per-user
- Public repo URLs for tools the skill depends on
- Public API endpoints that are conventions, not secrets (e.g., `localhost:31337/notify`)
- Example values clearly marked as placeholders (`<url>`, `<SESSION_ID>`, `test@example.com`)
- Generic env var *names* (never values): `STRIPE_API_KEY`, `OPENAI_API_KEY`

### Pre-Flight Grep (Public Skills Only)

Before shipping or modifying any `TitleCase` skill, run:
```bash
rg -i "<your-name>|<your-org>|<your-product>|<your-domain>|/Users/[a-z]+/" ~/.claude/skills/<SkillName>/
```

Zero matches = ready for public release. Any match = either scrub it, move it to SKILLCUSTOMIZATIONS, or rename the skill to `_ALLCAPS` and stop pretending it's public. **`_ALLCAPS` skills are exempt from this grep — they are private by design.**

**CRITICAL: Keep folder structure FLAT - maximum 2 levels deep.**

### The Rule

**Maximum depth:** `skills/SkillName/Category/`

### ✅ ALLOWED (2 levels max)

```

skills/SkillName/Workflows/Create.md         # Workflow - one level deep - GOOD

**These subdirectories are allowed:**

## Dynamic Loading Pattern (Large Skills)

**For skills with SKILL.md > 100 lines:** Use dynamic loading to reduce context on skill invocation.

### How Loading Works

**Session startup:** Only frontmatter loads for routing
**Skill invocation:** Full SKILL.md loads
**Context files:** Load only when workflows reference them

### The Pattern

**SKILL.md** = Minimal (30-50 lines) - loads on skill invocation
- YAML frontmatter with triggers
- Brief description
- Workflow routing table
- Quick reference
- Pointers to context files

**Additional .md files** = Context files - SOPs for specific aspects (loaded on-demand)
- These are Standard Operating Procedures, not just documentation
- They provide specific handling instructions
- Can reference Workflows/, Tools/, etc.

### 🚨 CRITICAL: NO Context/ Subdirectory 🚨

**NEVER create Context/ or Docs/ subdirectories.**

Additional .md files ARE the context files. They live **directly in skill root**.

**WRONG:**
```
skills/Art/
├── SKILL.md
└── Context/              ❌ NEVER CREATE THIS
    └── Aesthetic.md
```

**CORRECT:**
```
skills/Art/
├── SKILL.md
├── Aesthetic.md          ✅ Context file in skill root
├── Examples.md           ✅ Context file in skill root
└── Tools.md              ✅ Context file in skill root
```

**The skill directory IS the context.**

### Example Structure

```
skills/Art/
├── SKILL.md              # 40 lines - minimal routing
├── Aesthetic.md          # Context file - SOP for aesthetic
├── Examples.md           # Context file - SOP for examples
├── Tools.md              # Context file - SOP for tools
├── Workflows/            # Workflows
│   └── Essay.md
└── Tools/                # CLI tools
    └── Generate.ts

## Skill Writing Guidance

When writing or improving skill instructions, follow these principles from Anthropic's skill-creator methodology and Thariq Shihipar's "Lessons from Building Claude Code" (Mar 2026):

### Core Principles

- **Don't state the obvious.** Claude is competent at programming and knows codebases. Focus on information that **breaks Claude's default patterns** — things it gets wrong without guidance. Test: "Would Claude do this wrong without being told?" If not, remove it.
- **Explain the why, not just the what.** Models with good theory of mind + clear reasoning outperform models with rigid constraints. Instead of "ALWAYS use 3 bullets", explain why bullets matter for the audience.
- **Keep it lean.** The context window is a public good. Remove instructions that don't improve output. If test transcripts show the agent wasting time on unproductive steps, cut them. SKILL.md should be under 500 lines.
- **Cut intensifier-only lines.** Stating a rule once is the instruction. `MANDATORY`, `CRITICAL`, "not optional", and a third restatement add volume, not constraint — the model obeys specificity and code, not emphasis. Delete any line whose only content is shouting a rule stated elsewhere. Watch `## Best Practices` / `## Tips` sections: they collect default-restating filler ("be thorough", "keep it simple", "validate carefully"). Run the delete-test in `Prompting/Standards.md` § Signal-to-Noise on every line: cut it, and restore only if you can name the specific non-default behavior it forces.
- **Generalize, don't overfit.** Fix underlying patterns, not specific test failures. The skill will be used on many prompts beyond your test set.
- **Bundle repeated work.** If test agents all independently wrote similar helper scripts, add that script to Tools/ so every future invocation benefits.
- **Set appropriate degrees of freedom.** Match specificity to task fragility. Database migrations need exact commands; code reviews need general direction.
- **Don't over-constrain.** Skills are reused heavily. Avoid overly specific instructions. Provide needed information but leave flexibility for different contexts.

### Description Best Practices

- **Descriptions are for models, not humans.** The description is injected into the system prompt. Claude reads it to decide whether to invoke the skill.
- **Descriptions should be slightly pushy.** Models tend to undertrigger. Name specific scenarios even if the user might not explicitly mention the skill.
- **Include negative triggers for confusable skills.** Add "NOT FOR" clauses when skills share vocabulary: `"NOT FOR web pentesting (use WebAssessment)"`.
- **Undertriggering signals:** Skill doesn't load when it should, users manually invoking it.
- **Overtriggering signals:** Skill loads for irrelevant queries, users disabling it.

### Gotchas Section (MANDATORY)

Every skill MUST have a `## Gotchas` section after the workflow routing table. Thariq: "The highest information density in any Skill comes from gotchas sections."

Populate with:
- API quirks Claude doesn't know about
- Common mistakes observed during usage
- Ordering/sequencing requirements that aren't obvious
- Edge cases that cause silent failures

**Gotchas accumulate over time.** After every skill failure, add the lesson.

### BPE (Bitter-Pilled Engineering) Check

Before finalizing any skill, ask: **"Would a smarter model make this skill unnecessary?"**

- **Anti-fragile (keep):** Verification harnesses, data pipelines, tool wrappers, accumulated gotchas, deterministic scripts
- **Fragile (question):** CoT orchestrators, format parsers, retry cascades, elaborate reasoning scaffolding

Focus skills on knowledge Claude can't derive (failure modes, API quirks), tools Claude can't replicate (API calls, automation), and workflows that benefit from consistency.

### Progressive Disclosure (from Anthropic)

Three levels of information loading — use this to manage large skills:
1. **Level 1 (YAML frontmatter):** Always in system prompt. Triggering info only.
2. **Level 2 (SKILL.md body):** Loaded when skill is invoked. Routing + key guidance.
3. **Level 3 (Reference files):** Root-level `.md` files or `References/` subdirectory loaded on demand.

Tell Claude what files exist; it will read them when appropriate. SKILL.md should be under 500 lines — if over, extract detailed content to reference files.

### Testing Best Practices (from Anthropic)

Three testing levels for skills:
1. **Manual testing** — Run queries and observe behavior
2. **Scripted testing** — Automate test cases (use TestSkill workflow)
3. **Programmatic testing** — Build evaluation suites (use Evals skill)

**Evaluation-driven development:** Define what "this skill working" looks like before building the skill. Iterate on a single challenging task until Claude succeeds, then extract the winning approach.

### On-Demand Hook Pattern (from Anthropic)

Skills can include hooks that activate only when invoked, remaining effective for the session:
- `/careful` — Intercept dangerous commands (rm -rf, DROP TABLE, force-push)
- `/freeze` — Block edits outside specific directories
- `/audit` — Log all tool calls for session review

*All guidance above derived from Thariq Shihipar's "Lessons from Building Claude Code" (Mar 2026), Anthropic's official skill guide, and platform documentation.*
